The doctor was elderly, and when I woke him he looked like a very pleasant, kindly old fellow. I told him my brother and me had been hunting on Spanish Island yesterday afternoon and had camped on a bit of raft we found. Around midnight my brother must have kicked his gun while dreaming, because it fired and hit his leg. We wanted the doctor to come over and mend it, without saying a word or letting anybody hear, because we meant to get home that evening and surprise our folks.

“Who are your folks?” he asked.

“The Phelpses, down that way.”

“Oh,” he said. After a little he asked:

“How did you say he came to get shot?”

“He was having a dream,” I said, “and it shot him.”

“A remarkable dream,” he said.

Then he lighted his lantern, fetched his saddle-bags, and we set out. But he didn't fancy the canoe when he saw it. He said it would hold one well enough, but didn't seem very safe for two. I said:

“No need to worry, sir. She carried all three of us without trouble.”

“Which three?”

“Me and Sid, of course, and—and—and the guns. That's what I meant.”

“Oh,” he said.

But he set a foot on the gunwale and rocked her, then shook his head and said he'd better look for something larger. All the other boats were chained and locked, though. So he took mine and told me to wait for his return, or keep looking, or perhaps go home and prepare everybody for the surprise, if I liked. I said I didn't want to. I explained exactly where the raft lay, and off he went.

Before long a thought struck me. Suppose, I said to myself, he can't mend that leg in three shakes of a sheep's tail, as folks say? Suppose it takes three or four days? Are we to sit there till he spills the whole secret? Not me. I know what I'll do. I'll wait here, and if he comes back saying he must make another visit, I'll get to the raft too, even if I have to swim. We'll tie him up and keep him, and drift on downriver. Once Tom has no more need of him, we'll pay what his work is worth, or every cent we've got, and put him ashore.

Then I crawled into a pile of lumber for a sleep. Next thing I knew, the sun was high overhead! I jumped out and hurried to the doctor's house, but they said he'd left sometime in the night and hadn't returned.

The Attorney-General told the jury that the prisoner was young in age but experienced in the acts of treason for which he deserved to die. His dealings with the enemy had not begun today, yesterday, last year, or even the year before. For longer than that, the prisoner had repeatedly travelled between France and England on secret business he could not honestly explain. If treason could prosper—which, fortunately, it never could—the true evil and guilt of his activities might have stayed hidden. But Providence had inspired a fearless man of spotless character to uncover the prisoner’s plans. Horrified by what he found, this man had reported them to His Majesty’s Chief Secretary of State and most honorable Privy Council. This patriot would appear before the jury. His conduct was, on the whole, magnificent. He had been the prisoner’s friend, but in an hour both fortunate and terrible he had discovered the man’s wickedness. He had then decided to sacrifice on his country’s sacred altar the traitor he could no longer hold dear. If Britain awarded statues to public benefactors, as ancient Greece and Rome had done, this outstanding citizen would certainly have received one. Since Britain did not, he probably would not. Virtue, as poets had observed, was in a way contagious, especially that shining virtue called patriotism, or love of country. The Attorney-General referred to many poetic passages that he assured the jury they must know word for word. The jurors’ faces betrayed a guilty awareness that they knew none of them. The noble example of this perfect, unquestionable witness for the Crown—a man it was an honor even to mention, however inadequately—had inspired the prisoner’s servant. It had filled him with a sacred determination to search his master’s desk drawers and pockets and secretly remove his papers. The Attorney-General expected that someone would try to criticize this admirable servant. Generally speaking, however, he preferred the man to his own brothers and sisters, and respected him more than his own father and mother. He confidently urged the jury to feel the same. The testimony of these two witnesses, together with the documents they had discovered and would present, would prove that the prisoner had possessed lists of His Majesty’s forces. These included details of their positions and preparations, both on land and at sea. The evidence would leave no doubt that he had regularly passed this information to an enemy power.

“Just then, both he and I noticed the scrap of parchment, which I took for paper at the time. It lay half buried in the sand, with one corner showing. Nearby I saw the remains of what seemed to be the hull of a ship’s longboat. The wreck must have been there for a very long time, because its pieces were barely recognizable as boat timbers.

“Jupiter picked up the parchment, wrapped the beetle in it, and handed it to me. Soon afterward we headed home and met Lieutenant G—— along the way. I showed him the insect, and he begged to borrow it and take it to the fort. When I agreed, he immediately pushed it into his waistcoat pocket without its wrapping. I had kept hold of the parchment while he examined the beetle. Perhaps he was afraid I would change my mind and wanted to secure his prize at once. You know how excited he gets about anything to do with natural history. At the same time, I must have slipped the parchment into my own pocket without noticing.

“You remember that when I went to the table to draw the beetle, there was no paper in its usual place. I checked the drawer and found none there either. Then I searched my pockets, hoping to find an old letter, and my hand came upon the parchment. I am explaining exactly how I acquired it because those circumstances struck me with unusual force.

“You will probably think I am letting my imagination run away with me. But I had already made a connection, joining two links in what might be a much longer chain. A boat lay on the seashore, and close to it was a piece of parchment—not paper—with a skull drawn on it. Naturally, you will ask what connects these things. My answer is that a skull is the well-known symbol of pirates. They raise a flag bearing a skull whenever they fight.

“I have stressed that the scrap was parchment rather than paper. Parchment lasts a long time; it is almost impossible to destroy through age. People seldom use it for unimportant things, since ordinary paper is much better suited to everyday writing and drawing. Thinking about this suggested that the skull had some meaning, some purpose. I also noticed the parchment’s shape. Although an accident had destroyed one corner, it was still clear that the piece had originally been a rectangle longer than it was wide.”
